papers.title: Reducing sprint time with exosuit assistance in the real world
papers.authors_short: Moon, Nam, Ryu, Kim, Yun, Yang, Yang, Lee
papers.code_status: No controller code or raw data found. Zenodo holds only the supplementary materials (4 DataCite versions, CC BY 4.0); its description lists Tables S1-S4, but the KB's 7-page local copy has S1-S3 (Zenodo files not opened: HTTP 403, 2026-09-23).
papers.api_title: Reducing sprint time with exosuit assistance in the real world
papers.core_idea: Portable Bowden-cable exosuit assists hip extension with a fixed, IMU-timed admittance force profile during outdoor 200 m sprints. Nine non-elite men ran 0.97±0.41 s (SEM) faster; first 100 m gain significant (0.68 s), second 100 m not (0.30 s); step-frequency change correlated with gain.
papers.what_to_take: Comparator device: force onset/peak/release at 2/30/45% of the cycle after maximum hip flexion, peak 20–35% body weight, assumed 0.15 m moment arm; 32.79→31.82 s group means (≈6.1 m/s average).
papers.left_untested: Only suit-on vs no-suit (no unpowered-suit arm), so mass and assistance are confounded; no hip-flexion arm, fatigue or metabolic measure; per-trial wind unreported; two of nine slowed.
papers.feasibility_notes: Supplement suffices to rebuild the force-profile controller as a sim comparator; no raw data or code, so fit is to published means only.

papers.title: Lambda-Hold Control: Human-Like Movement Emerges from a Minimal Task Reward in Predictive Musculoskeletal Simulation
papers.code_status: Not released: project page shows 'Code (TBA)' and 'Paper (TBA)'; no matching repository among the first author's GitHub repos (checked 2026-09-23).
papers.api_title: Lambda-Hold Control: Human-Like Movement Emerges from a Minimal Task Reward in Predictive Musculoskeletal Simulation
papers.core_idea: Policy outputs per-muscle equilibrium-point thresholds λ; a stretch-reflex law converts them to excitations, held 0.05–0.15 s between GRF-event decisions. SAC+gSDE on H2190 (90 muscles, SCONE/Hyfydy) learns standing-start sprinting from reward exp(vx)·lateral penalty; ~4.7 m/s top speed.
papers.what_to_take: Baseline targets: ~4.7 m/s top speed, ~4.0 m/s after ~1 h on RTX 5070; mean EMG correlation 0.42. Speed ceiling: psoas/iliacus reach only 0.26/0.33 isometric force; Vmax 10→20 gives ~6.5 m/s.
papers.left_untested: Two seeds only; no arms; no fatigue model; no 200 m distance, split or timing analysis; knee and hip flexion fall below human data at speed; vasti and tibialis anterior timing wrong; no device coupling.
papers.feasibility_notes: Hyfydy is a licensed engine; a MuJoCo/MyoLeg port must re-derive the λ reflex law and GRF-event holds and re-validate the 4.7 m/s ceiling.

papers.title: Learning Realistic Athletic Sprinting Without Demonstrations
papers.authors_short: Wang, Bianco, Tevet, Hicks, Liu, Delp, Fatahalian
papers.venue: SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 (to appear, per project page); arXiv 2026-09-10. ACM DOI 10.1145/3829340.3842159 is listed by arXiv but did not resolve at doi.org or Crossref on 2026-09-23
papers.code_status: Released: willwng/bolt (NVIDIA Warp simulator, last push 2026-08-26) and willwng/msk_envs (RL environments, last push 2026-08-24); GitHub detects no licence in either repo (checked 2026-09-23).
papers.api_title: Learning Realistic Athletic Sprinting Without Demonstrations
papers.core_idea: Bolt, a Warp GPU simulator of OpenSim-grade Hill muscles with elastic tendons (~1000× real time), trains FastTD3 policies emitting 136-muscle excitations at 30 Hz from reward v_x − w·joint-limit torque + alive. A calibrated sprinter model runs a full 100 m without demonstrations.
papers.what_to_take: Benchmarks and warnings: ~10 s 100 m, 12.5±0.5 m/s peak (data 9.65), GRF ~2 BW high; MuJoCo solver constraints and rigid tendons degraded sprint gaits; under a day on one RTX 6000 PRO.
papers.left_untested: No fatigue (maximal output held for 100 m), no 200 m race, no exoskeleton or device coupling; results reported from the best of up to five seeds; EMG checked only as on/off timing.
papers.feasibility_notes: Code runs on one NVIDIA GPU; an RTX 5090 (32 GB) is likely adequate but untested; 26M-sample on-GPU replay buffer needs memory planning.

papers.title: Muscular strategy shift in human running: dependence of running speed on hip and ankle muscle performance
papers.code_status: No code or data link in API records; full text not checked. (Crossref also lists 10.1242/jeb.075051, a same-title record at 215(13):2347, likely a correction.)
papers.api_title: Muscular strategy shift in human running: dependence of running speed on hip and ankle muscle performance
papers.core_idea: Nine runners' data, slow running to maximal sprinting, drove a musculoskeletal model. Below ~7 m/s, soleus and gastrocnemius supply support, lengthening strides; above it they shorten too fast, and iliopsoas, gluteus maximus and hamstrings raise stride frequency via faster swing.
papers.what_to_take: The ~7 m/s strategy-shift threshold: a 4.7 m/s simulated sprinter sits in the ankle-dominated, stride-length regime, so hip-assist mechanisms from real sprinters (>7 m/s) may not appear; track stride length versus frequency separately.
papers.left_untested: Constant-speed trials only, not acceleration or a 200 m; no fatigue; muscle contributions computed from data-tracking simulations, not predicted; no external assistance tested.
papers.feasibility_notes: Paper-only; use as a validation target: simulated plantarflexor versus hip-muscle contributions to support and swing across speed bins.

papers.title: Limitations to maximum sprinting speed imposed by muscle mechanical properties
papers.code_status: No code found (abstract and API records only).
papers.api_title: Limitations to maximum sprinting speed imposed by muscle mechanical properties
papers.core_idea: Maximum-speed 2D Hill-muscle sprinting simulations were rerun with single muscle properties removed: removing force–velocity raised speed 15%, excitation–activation 8%, force–length 4%; removing series elasticity cut speed 26%; ideal joint torques gave +22%.
papers.what_to_take: Sanity bounds for the Hill-model ceiling: removing force–velocity adds 15% top speed; removing tendon elasticity costs 26%, so rigid-tendon MuJoCo muscles need a check before any assisted-speed claim.
papers.left_untested: 2D model with lumped muscles; no acceleration, 200 m or fatigue; properties removed wholesale rather than bounded; no external assistive torque or device limits.
papers.feasibility_notes: Cheap to replicate as ablations in the reimplemented model (force–velocity off, Vmax scaled): diagnostics only, never in the assisted condition alone.

papers.title: Simulating Ideal Assistive Devices to Reduce the Metabolic Cost of Running
papers.authors_short: Uchida, Seth, Pouya, Dembia, Hicks, Delp
papers.code_status: Per Data Availability: simulations/data at simtk.org/home/idealassist_run, metabolics plug-in at github.com/opensim-org/opensim-metabolicsprobes; SimTK did not respond on 2026-09-23 (not re-checked).
papers.api_title: Simulating Ideal Assistive Devices to Reduce the Metabolic Cost of Running
papers.core_idea: CMC simulations of 10 runners at 2 and 5 m/s (OpenSim, 92 muscles) add massless, lossless, unlimited ideal torque actuators at hip, knee and/or ankle while tracking unassisted kinematics and GRFs, then compare predicted muscle metabolic power.
papers.what_to_take: Speed flips the best joint: ideal hip flexion/extension saves 25±2%→33±4% (2→5 m/s) while ankle falls 26±4%→19±4%; peak mean hip torque 3.5 N·m/kg, the unconstrained reference for limited devices.
papers.left_untested: Kinematics and GRFs are fixed, so speed or sprint-time changes cannot emerge; no device mass, torque, power or tension limits; nothing above 5 m/s; no acceleration.
papers.feasibility_notes: Reproducible in OpenSim from public data; for sprinting, rerun predictively (not tracking) with the same ideal hip actuator as the upper bound.

papers.title: Predictive Simulations of Human Sprinting: Effects of Muscle–Tendon Properties on Sprint Performance
papers.code_status: No code found (abstract and API records only).
papers.api_title: Predictive Simulations of Human Sprinting: Effects of Muscle–Tendon Properties on Sprint Performance
papers.core_idea: A 3D, 86-muscle predictive dynamic optimization of maximum-speed sprinting, seeded from a jogging solution, varies lower-limb strength, fascicle length, intrinsic maximum shortening velocity and tendon compliance to rank their effect on top speed.
papers.what_to_take: Sensitivity table for parity checks: +10% strength → +5.9% top speed; fascicle length +4.7%; Vmax +2.4%; tendon compliance +0.3%. Any assisted-only change to these would swamp a 2–3% exo effect.
papers.left_untested: Maximum-speed gait only: no standing start, 200 m or fatigue; no external assistance; properties changed across lower-limb muscles together, not per group.
papers.feasibility_notes: No code; use the numbers as external checks on the reimplemented model's speed sensitivity (e.g., a +10% Vmax diagnostic run).

papers.title: Modifications to the net knee moments lead to the greatest improvements in accelerative sprinting performance: a predictive simulation study
papers.code_status: Figshare dataset described as 'Data files, model and videos'; solver code not mentioned in that description (description checked only, 2026-09-23).
papers.api_title: Modifications to the net knee moments lead to the greatest improvements in accelerative sprinting performance: a predictive simulation study
papers.core_idea: Direct-collocation (CasADi/IPOPT) 3D model (92 muscles) scaled to an international sprinter tracks, then predicts, the first acceleration steps with net ankle, knee and/or hip moments freed; performance is average horizontal external power.
papers.what_to_take: Ideal-moment upper bounds for early acceleration: knee-free +13.8%, knee+hip-free +21.9%, all-free +22.0% (1401 vs 1149 W); hip-free gains were smaller, bounding what a hip-only device can add early.
papers.left_untested: Only the first few acceleration steps; freed net moments carry no device limits (tension, power, delay, mass); no top-speed phase, 200 m, fatigue or human validation.
papers.feasibility_notes: MATLAB/CasADi collocation suits the EPYC CPU; transferring the 'free-moment' idea to RL means adding an ideal hip actuator arm.

papers.title: Faster top running speeds are achieved with greater ground forces not more rapid leg movements
papers.api_title: Faster top running speeds are achieved with greater ground forces not more rapid leg movements
papers.core_idea: Treadmill force-plate measurements in 33 runners (top speeds 6.2–11.1 m/s) and in inclined/declined top-speed running show faster runners apply larger stance-averaged vertical forces (1.26× from 6.2 to 11.1 m/s) while minimum swing time does not vary.
papers.what_to_take: Mechanism readouts for any simulated gain: stance-averaged force/body weight, contact time and swing time. Weyand 2010 adds the contact-time limit: ~0.11 s and ~2.1 BW at top forward speed.
papers.left_untested: Mostly correlational (plus an incline/decline contrast); treadmill top speed only; no acceleration or fatigue; no muscle-level cause; no assistance. Conflicts with simulation claims that hip-driven swing sets stride frequency above 7 m/s.
papers.feasibility_notes: Paper-only; the three scalar metrics are computable from any simulated GRF trace.

papers.title: Musculoskeletal Motion Imitation for Learning Personalized Exoskeleton Control Policy in Impaired Gait
papers.code_status: No code link in arXiv v1 (checked 2026-09-23).
papers.api_title: Musculoskeletal Motion Imitation for Learning Personalized Exoskeleton Control Policy in Impaired Gait
papers.core_idea: An H2190 (90-muscle) human in Hyfydy is trained with SAC to imitate single-subject treadmill gait (0.6–2.2 m/s), then given ideal sagittal hip, knee and ankle torque actuators plus device mass (hip exo 2.9 kg) to cut simulated metabolic cost, including deficit models.
papers.what_to_take: Expectation anchor: hip assistance cut simulated metabolic cost only 6.95% in running (ankle 13.81%); compute anchor: 96 Hyfydy envs, 600M SAC steps, ~48 h on an RTX 5090.
papers.left_untested: Running only to 2.2 m/s; metabolic cost, not speed, is the objective; ideal motors without tension-only, delay or power limits; single reference subject; no hardware test.
papers.feasibility_notes: Same H2190/Hyfydy stack as Lambda-Hold and the same GPU class; no code, so reimplementation from the paper only.

papers.title: Modification of a three-compartment muscle fatigue model to predict peak torque decline during intermittent tasks
papers.code_status: No official code. Third-party: MyoSuite CumulativeFatigue (3CC-r via Cheema et al. CHI 2020 / User-in-the-Box), defaults F=0.00912, R=0.1×0.00094, r=150, plus an MJX variant fatigue_jax.py (checked 2026-09-23).
papers.api_title: Modification of a three-compartment muscle fatigue model to predict peak torque decline during intermittent tasks
papers.core_idea: Adds a rest-recovery multiplier r to the three-compartment (resting/active/fatigued) controller fatigue model; fitted to 351 intermittent isometric torque-decline points from 63 studies, cutting prediction error from 19–29% to 6–10% torque decline.
papers.what_to_take: Joint parameters: ankle F=0.00589, R=0.00058; knee F=0.0150, R=0.00149; r=15 (no hip data). MyoSuite's default is elbow-based, so lower-limb values must be set explicitly.
papers.left_untested: Isometric intermittent tasks only; dynamic contractions excluded; no hip or trunk data; no fibre-type dependence; never validated for sprinting or 20–40 s maximal efforts.
papers.feasibility_notes: Three ODEs per muscle, trivially batched on GPU; the real cost is calibrating against sprint speed-decay data.

papers.api_title: PositiveAssist: Energy-Gated Control for Positive Power Assistance of Exoskeleton in Walking, Running, and Stair Climbing

papers.title: MetaboliSim: a Python implementation of the Mader model for dynamic and steady-state simulation of muscular energy metabolism
papers.code_status: Released (AGPL-3.0 per paper): Codeberg repo created 2026-03-28, updated 2026-09-10; metabolisim.org responds (checked 2026-09-23).
papers.api_title: MetaboliSim: a Python implementation of the Mader model for dynamic and steady-state simulation of muscular energy metabolism
papers.core_idea: Open Python implementation of the Mader model of muscular energy metabolism: a five-state ODE (phosphate potential, VO2, muscle and blood lactate, glycogen) integrated by RK4, plus steady-state MLSS equations; verified against published reference values and checked for plausibility on sprint and running protocols.
papers.what_to_take: A whole-body energy budget for a 20–40 s maximal effort: couple simulated mechanical power demand to phosphocreatine and glycolytic supply to cap late-race power instead of inventing a fatigue law.
papers.left_untested: Not a muscle-level model; no coupling to musculoskeletal simulation; sprint behaviour checked for plausibility only; VO2max and VLamax are athlete inputs.
papers.feasibility_notes: Pure Python and cheap to run; the AGPL licence affects redistribution of combined code.

cluster_lessons: The simulated speed ceiling belongs to the muscle model, not the controller. In Lambda-Hold (2608.17030), H2190 tops out near 4.7 m/s because fully active psoas/iliacus produce only 0.26/0.33 of isometric force at their fastest shortening, and doubling Vmax (10→20 optimal lengths/s) gives ~6.5 m/s. Removing force–velocity in Miller et al. 2012 adds 15%. That makes swing-phase hip-flexion assistance a direct test of the planned human model's bottleneck, even though Moon assisted extension.

Parity matters more than usual. Lin & Pandy 2022 show that +10% strength gives +5.9% top speed and +10% Vmax gives +2.4%, while Moon's human effect is only ~3% of 200 m time (0.97 of 32.79 s). A strength or Vmax change applied to the assisted condition alone would swamp any device effect. Keep such changes as symmetric diagnostics only.

Speed regimes do not line up. Lambda-Hold's 4.7 m/s top speed is below the ~6.1 m/s average 200 m speed of Moon's non-elite runners and far below Dorn et al.'s ~7 m/s shift to a hip-driven stride-frequency strategy. Bolt's sprinter peaks at 12.5±0.5 m/s against 9.65 m/s in the comparison data. Only percentage change against the same model's own unassisted baseline carries over between models, and even that needs a check across plant speeds.

Hip versus ankle depends on the phase. At steady high speed, hip extensor/knee flexor terminal-swing loads rise most (Schache 2011), and the ideal hip actuator beats ankle/knee at 5 m/s (Uchida 2016: 33±4%). During acceleration, however, the ankle supplies the most positive work (Schache 2019, JEB, 1.55±0.17 J/kg), and freeing knee moments helps most (Haralabidis 2022). Yet Moon's significant gain was in the first 100 m. Report 0–30/30–60/60–100/100–200 m splits.

Ideal-device studies cannot predict sprint time. Uchida fixes kinematics and GRFs (metabolic savings only), and Haralabidis frees net joint moments with no device limits. The step from 'ideal' to 'realizable' (tension-only, attachment-dependent moment arm, delay, torque-speed-power limits, mass) has not been simulated for sprinting, and Ciaramella's −9.6% vs −4.3% net shows how much wearing the unpowered suit costs.

Contact and constraint modelling can decide whether sprinting emerges at all. Bolt reports that MuJoCo's solver-based joint limits/contacts gave unstable sprints (lateral foot drift, stride variance), that rigid tendons increased stride-frequency variance, and that uncalibrated passive forces were exploited through hip rotation. Miller finds tendon elasticity worth 26% of top speed. The planned MuJoCo/MyoLeg port therefore needs an unassisted equivalence check against H2190/Hyfydy before any exosuit run.

No sprint simulation models fatigue. Bolt holds maximal output for 100 m, and Lambda-Hold has no fatigue term. 3CC-r (Looft 2018) is calibrated on isometric ankle/knee/elbow/grip data only (r=15; no hip), and MyoSuite's default uses elbow values. A 200 m model therefore either adds an uncalibrated per-muscle fatigue law or a whole-body energy budget (Mader model, MetaboliSim). That choice determines whether any second-half benefit can appear.

Non-learned comparators already exist and should be matched on limits: Moon's fixed profile (2/30/45% after max hip flexion, 20–35% BW peak, 0.15 m arm), PositiveAssist's energy gate (>94.8% positive power in running up to 3.5 m/s), and Foggetti et al.'s stride-wise timing optimizer (BioRob 2026, +6.1–17.2% positive work offline). Passive tension-only baselines include Simpson's exotendon (6.4%), Yang's hip-flexion bands (4.7%, 609 g) and Nasiri's inter-hip spring (TNSRE 2018, 8.0±1.5% at 2.5 m/s).
occupied_claims: Hip-extension exosuit reduces real-world 200 m sprint time: 0.97±0.41 s (SEM), n=9 non-elite men, significant only in the first 100 m. Moon et al., Science Robotics 2023 (10.1126/scirobotics.adf5611).

Demonstration-free RL of a muscle-driven full 100 m sprint (~10 s, 12.5 m/s peak) on one GPU with an open Warp simulator, plus the finding that MuJoCo solver constraints degrade sprint gaits. Wang et al., arXiv 2609.11083 (SIGGRAPH Asia 2026).

Minimal-reward RL sprinting from a standing start in a 90-muscle model within ~1 h via equilibrium-point λ holds, with the hip-flexor force–velocity ceiling (4.7→6.5 m/s) identified. Lee, Lee, Ahn, arXiv 2608.17030.
RL-trained ideal hip/ankle exo torques in an H2190 human cut simulated running metabolic cost 6.95%/13.81% (≤2.2 m/s). Choi et al., arXiv 2604.09431.
The ideal hip actuator is the most effective single joint at 5 m/s running (33±4% simulated metabolic saving). Uchida et al., PLOS ONE 2016.

Predictive optimal-control sprint studies: freeing knee/hip net moments raises early-acceleration power 13.8–22% (Haralabidis et al. 2022); top-speed sensitivity to strength, fascicle length, Vmax and tendon compliance (Lin & Pandy 2022; Miller et al. 2012, 2D).
Energy-gated positive-power hip exoskeleton control that works across walking and running up to 3.5 m/s without retuning. Zhou et al., IEEE/ASME TMECH 2026 (PositiveAssist).

Soft-suit sprint augmentation programme with a stated goal of a 7 s 100 m for an average (17 s) runner, using pneumatic artificial muscles and a hybrid energy system. DASH, Yonsei HCAIR (Prof. Dongjun Shin), programme page https://hcr.yonsei.ac.kr/research/Human-Robotic-Mobilities/ALC/. The lab's publication list shows related work (a pneumatic jump-enhancement soft suit, Adv Intell Syst 8(2); running aerodynamics and required power, Int J Appl Mech 15(1)) but no sprint-assist result.
open_gaps: Primary endpoint unoccupied (search result, not proof): no study found simulates an actuator-limited, tension-only hip exosuit (moment arm, delay, torque-speed-power limits, mass) and reports a change in simulated 200 m (or any sprint) time. Run it against the ideal-hip-actuator upper bound and a mass-only (unpowered) arm.

Flexion versus extension at sprint speed: the model's bottleneck is hip-flexor force–velocity in swing (Lambda-Hold), but the only human sprint evidence assisted extension (Moon). No human or simulation study compares matched-limit flexion, extension and bidirectional assistance for sprint time.

Phase decomposition: no simulation splits an assisted sprint gain into standing-start acceleration, top-speed and fatigue phases, or checks Moon's first-100 m pattern. Log 10 m splits, contact time, stance-averaged force/BW and swing time (Weyand), and ratio of forces (Morin 2011).

Fatigue for a 200 m: there are no dynamic-contraction or hip 3CC-r parameters, and no sprint RL paper models fatigue. Calibrate a fatigue or energy-budget layer against published 200 m velocity decay before claiming second-half effects, and report results with and without it.

Plant-speed transfer: no work tests whether an exo's percentage benefit measured on a 4.7 m/s plant holds on a faster plant. Repeat the best controller on a symmetric Vmax-curriculum (diagnostic) human and on Bolt's open sprinter model.

Engine sensitivity: Bolt's MuJoCo-constraint failure has not been tested on MyoLeg-style models with explicit device cables. Measure unassisted sprint speed, stride variance and lateral drift across solver settings and ≥5 seeds before the exosuit experiments (Lambda-Hold used 2 seeds; Bolt reported the best of up to 5).

Environment realism: neither Lambda-Hold nor Bolt mentions aerodynamic drag (full-text search). A 2026 on-site study (D'Angelo et al., Exp Fluids, 10.1007/s00348-026-04204-3) reports drag areas 30–40% below earlier estimates at 8 m/s, so check how sensitive the 200 m time is to drag at the model's speeds.
unverifiable: Seed URL hcr.yonsei.ac.kr/team/alchemist/dash_2024.html: HTTP 404 and no Wayback Machine capture (checked 2026-09-23). The DASH programme itself was verified at https://hcr.yonsei.ac.kr/research/Human-Robotic-Mobilities/ALC/ (page title 'DASH | Human-Centered AI Robotics Lab'). It is listed under occupied_claims rather than papers because it reports no data.

Seed 'Haugen et al. 2019 sprint running review (Sports Med)': no 2019 Haugen record in Sports Medicine was found. Two 2019 Haugen reviews were verified instead, 'Sprint running: from fundamental mechanics to practice—a review' (Eur J Appl Physiol 119:1273–1287, 10.1007/s00421-019-04139-0) and 'The Training and Development of Elite Sprint Performance…' (Sports Medicine - Open 5:44, 10.1186/s40798-019-0221-0). Neither was selected.

Seed 'Schache et al. 2011 hip muscle contributions': the only matching 2011 record is 'Effect of Running Speed on Lower Limb Joint Kinetics' (MSSE 43(7):1260–1271, 10.1249/mss.0b013e3182084929), which reports joint kinetics, not muscle contributions. Muscle-level contributions are in Dorn et al. 2012 (selected). Verified, not selected.

Seed 'MyoSuite fatigue model': no standalone MyoSuite fatigue paper was found. The implementation (myosuite/envs/myo/fatigue.py, CumulativeFatigue, 3CC-r adapted from Cheema et al. CHI 2020, 10.1145/3313831.3376701) was verified in code and is recorded under Looft et al. 2018.

Moon et al. supplement Table S4: the Zenodo description lists Tables S1–S4, but the KB's local supplement has S1–S3. Zenodo file access returned HTTP 403 (rate limit), so the content of any Table S4 is unverified.

Kim et al. 2019 exosuit hardware parameters (mass, peak force, actuator specs) could not be read (paywalled full text). Only the abstract numbers (−9.3% walking at 1.5 m/s, −4.0% running at 2.5 m/s) were verified, and none of the hardware figures were used.
